name: old cracked asphalt road of cool charcoal grey with fine scattered non-directional aggregate specks, faded slightly warmer patches, thin crack lines, soft stains and worn broken fragments of yellow and white lane paint, its unconnected edges broken off into dirt as a chipped asphalt lip with loose asphalt chunks, laid as a road network with crossroads and dead ends
label: wasteland_ruins/asphalt

surfaces.part: asphalt road network patches on dirt ground (flat terrain tile sheet)

answer.evidence: This is a terrain tile sheet: a full 256x192 opaque dirt ground with grey asphalt road pieces (crossroads, T-junctions, dead ends, a large block with cracks and a yellow lane-paint fragment). The roads are drawn flat from above. Their south edges have only a 1-2 row dark chipped lip. There is no vertical front face of 3+ rows, no ellipse and no roof. The width profile is 256 for every row, so there is no standing silhouette. The only thing to measure is a flat ground surface, with no front face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The asphalt reads as roughly 3 lightness steps (charcoal body, a lighter speck, a dark crack/edge) against about 6 on the paving reference. The tile measures 5 visible tones against 7 for paving and 3 for grass, so it is not far off on tone count. Dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the edges lean tinted rather than sticker-black, but the chipped lip is a thin dark line of one value with little step shading. Near-flat coverage is 5%, so large flat fills are mostly avoided, but the asphalt interiors are dominated by one grey with sparse specks, and the aggregate, stains and warmer patches the brief asks for are barely visible. The lane paint is only a single small yellow mark. The dirt surround has some mottling in 2-3 browns. Overall the piece is shallower in shading than the Beodeul paving: few ramp steps, a thin edge treatment and sparse texture. Under the when-in-doubt rule it fails.

surfaces.part: asphalt road patches (crossroad, T-junctions, dead ends, rectangular slab)
dark chipped lip along south edges of the asphalt

answer.evidence: The tile is a flat ground sheet: brown dirt with grey asphalt patches seen from straight above. The road pieces carry specks, cracks and lane-paint fragments across their whole surface. The only south-edge feature is a 1-row dark chipped lip under each patch. There is no front face of 3 or more rows and no vertical face, so it reads as a flat top-down slab. That is normal for a terrain tile.

styleAnswer.evidence: The asphalt reads as a flat charcoal slab with a thin darker edge, only about 3 visible steps (body, speckle, edge). The paving reference has about 7 tones with per-stone shading and highlights. The measured 5 visible tones per tile is below the paving reference (7) and above the grass (3), but the asphalt tones sit close together and look flatter than 5. The dirt surround carries the most variation, with brown speckle in a couple of shades. The cracks and lane paint are sparse: one yellow dash and a few cracks, with no worn white paint visible. The road patches are small, blobby and disconnected, so they do not read as a laid network with crossroads. Edge pixels are tinted (0% neutral), but the asphalt lip is a uniform dark band around each shape rather than shading that follows the material, so the outline is mixed. Large asphalt areas are mostly one grey with sparse specks, so flat fills remain in the road interior. Next to the paving reference it looks thinner and more sticker-like.

surfaces.part: asphalt road network (T-junctions, crossroads, dead ends, rectangular patch) on dirt ground

answer.evidence: This is a terrain tileset sheet, 256 wide by 192 tall and fully opaque. It is viewed from straight above, with asphalt road pieces on a brown dirt ground. The road shapes only have a 1-row dark chipped lip along their south edges, which is a thin edge shading line and not a vertical front face of 3 or more rows. The column scan shows only 1-4 row dark bands, which are cracks, edge lines and stains, and no tall front face. It reads as a flat top-down ground surface, which suits terrain, so the kind matches.

styleAnswer.evidence: The asphalt is mostly one flat charcoal with sparse specks and a few thin cracks. I count about 3 lightness steps on it: a base grey, a darker crack or speck tone, and a lighter speck. The paving reference has about 6-7 steps with per-stone shading and highlights. The dirt surround is better, with speckled brown grain, but it is also fairly uniform. Tile density is 5 visible tones against 7 for paving and 3 for grass. That is acceptable for a muted surface, though the asphalt itself reads thinner than the paving reference. The road chunks have dark edges, but they are a tinted dark grey, not pure black (0% neutral edge pixels). The edges are uniform and sticker-like, and the lip is only a simple dark rim with little chipped shading. Near-flat coverage is 5%, but visually the asphalt patches have broad plain areas. Yellow paint appears as one small fragment and the white paint is barely visible. Overall the piece is shallower than the Beodeul standard in shading steps and texture on its main material, so it fails.

surfaces.part: asphalt road pieces (crossroad, T-junctions, dead ends, straight, block) on dirt ground
large asphalt patch with cracks and yellow lane paint

answer.evidence: This is a flat top-down terrain sheet. The 256x192 image is covered by brown dirt with grey asphalt pieces on it. Each asphalt piece is a flat plan-view shape with speckles, cracks and a yellow lane-paint fragment. The only suggestion of depth is a 1-row dark lip along the south edge of each piece (for example around rows 43, 50 and 62). That is a single outline row, not a front face of 3 or more rows, and there is no eave shadow. No standing volume, side face or ellipse is drawn, so it reads as a top-down slab. As terrain it does not need a front face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The asphalt reads as only about 3 lightness steps: a charcoal base, one darker speck tone and a slightly lighter patch. It has 5 visible tones per tile and only 14 distinct colours in total, against a paving reference with 7 tones and many more shading steps. The asphalt interior shows large patches of nearly flat charcoal with sparse specks, and the thin cracks and the single yellow paint fragment are tiny. The dirt surround is better textured with mottling, but the road itself, which is the main subject, is shallow. The edge pixels are tinted, 0% neutral, so there is no pure near-black sticker line. Even so, the chipped lip is a uniform dark band with little per-chunk shading. The road pieces are also a sparse, fragmented layout, not a clearly connected network with crossroads. They look like cutout patches on a flat dirt field, less rich than the paving reference's stone-by-stone shading.
